title: What Is Sass?
learning_outcomes: Explain what is sass? and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply what is sass? in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **What Is Sass?** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect sass terminology with sass source files and compiled css, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: Sass extends CSS with a compile-time layer for reusable values, expressions, rules, and module organization. The compiler transforms the source file into ordinary CSS; the browser does not execute Sass syntax.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: Start with a small example, state the expected CSS behavior, compile it with Dart Sass, and compare the output with the intent. Retain the plain-CSS alternative when Sass adds no meaningful reuse or organization.

items.title: Sass terminology
items.text: Define the term in terms of what the compiler accepts and what CSS it emits; Sass is a source-language tool, not a browser runtime.

items.title: Sass source files and compiled CSS
items.text: Trace the source rule to its emitted CSS and inspect the output file. Treat the browser-facing CSS, not the SCSS source, as the final artifact.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with the smallest source file that demonstrates what is sass?. 2. State what should change and what should stay the same. 3. Compile the entrypoint with Dart Sass, or use the stated command if this lesson is about the toolchain. 4. Compare the resulting CSS or diagnostic with the expected result, then change one input and repeat.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small SCSS example that demonstrates what is sass?. Keep the example focused on one behavior, compile it with the version used by your project, and explain which part of the output proves your understanding.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

task: Create a small SCSS example that demonstrates what is sass?. Keep the example focused on one behavior, compile it with the version used by your project, and explain which part of the output proves your understanding.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes the intended Sass construct and a clear input.
The expected output or tool result is documented and consistent with the source.
The work is reproducible and includes one limitation, test, or troubleshooting note.
hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
